posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
I am afaid I lack knowledge to answer your questions, but perhaps some of mine will help.

1] John, I think you make your holograms broadband by pre-soaking them in water after illumination yes? It seems to me that the more narrow-band your hologram is, the more channels will fit.

2] Do you mean by multiple channels, the ability to store more images at different reference beam angles? If that is the case would it be possible to take an existing single channel (narrow-band) hologram and checking at what replay beam angle the image disappears? Would the next channel be available at double that angle? In that case the amount of channels would be approximately 180 degrees divided by 2 divided by the viewable angle. Then take three holograms with different thicknesses and calculate the possible amount of angles for each one and curve fit the results in a graph.

3] Does the amount of channels depend on the amount of information per channel? Is that the reason why an reflection H2 is more bright than a proper beam-ratio'ed Denisyuk?

posts.author: JohnFP
posts.content_md:
Hans as far as I have found, the soaking after exposure for broadband is only needed when the plates are not fresh, that is, greater then a day or so old which proves to be difficult with no soaking with old plates. Getting narrow band is rarely a problem with fresh or old plates.

Your number two statement is right on I believe so let me take the question one step further.

How many objects (w/seperate exposures) could be recorded with the same reference beam angle if the objects occupied the same location in space? 

And how many objects (w/separate exposures) could be recorded with the same reference beam angle if the objects occupied different locations in space?

If I wanted 5 different objects in my hologram, I could record them one by one with 5 individual exposures with the same reference angle. 

Now the question is, how many of these independent object holograms can I make before gross undesirables happen?

posts.author: Hans
posts.content_md:
> How many objects (w/seperate exposures) could be recorded with the same reference beam angle if the objects occupied the same location in space?

It seems to me that this depends on the complexity and the size of the objects. I guess with more objects and exposures the sacrifice is in detail/noise and brightness.

> And how many objects (w/separate exposures) could be recorded with the same reference beam angle if the objects occupied different locations in space?

Since object and reference beam are interchangable, I believe that comes back to my second question. By testing the reference beam angle at wich a single channle narrow-band holoram disappears, one should be able to calculate this. I think also the direction at wich the objects reflect have an effect. Do the objects reflect towards the whole surface of the plate or do they each reflect only to a different part of the plate?

Perhaps the best way to test this is with mirrors as objects and then measure the DE of each mirror in the final hologram?

I don't want to move to silver H1's for a couple of reasons.
